name: National liberalism
summary: National liberalism fuses liberal demands for constitutional government, rule of law and a free economy with the project of building a strong nation-state. Its motto in Germany was that national unity and freedom must be won together by the same means, through gradual, constitutional reform rather than revolution. In practice it was a party of the educated and propertied middle class and big business, which backed a monarchical constitution, strong national power, the Kulturkampf against clerical influence, and, increasingly, military and colonial expansion.
scope: The German National Liberal Party of 1867 to 1918 (Bennigsen, Lasker, Miquel; later Bassermann and early Stresemann), based on its June 1867 founding programme and the scholarship and reference accounts of the party. Mulej treats this party as the prime example of Central European 'national liberalism': liberal demands for constitutional order, civil liberties and equality before the law joined to nation-building, with the state as central as liberty. It excludes other national-liberal traditions (Austrian, Nordic, Romanian, Israeli, Korean and others) and the later nationalist drift after 1890, which Mulej describes as the 'national' overtaking the 'liberal'. The National Liberal Federations of Britain, Canada and India are separate liberal party organisations that share only the name and are out of scope.
